poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Trip upon trenchers, and dance upon dishes,
My mother sent me for some barm, some barm;
She bid me tread lightly, and come again quickly,
For fear the young men should do me some harm.
  Yet didn't you see, yet didn't you see,
  What naughty tricks they put upon me:

  They broke my pitcher,
    And spilt the water,
  And huff'd my mother,
    And chid her daughter,
And kiss'd my sister instead of me.

poems.title: Some up, and some down
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Some up, and some down,
    There's players in the town,
You wot well who they be;
    The sun doth arise,
    To three companies,
One, two, three, four, make wee!

    Besides we that travel,
    With pumps full of gravel,
Made all of such running leather:
    That once in a week,
    New masters we seek,
And never can hold together.

poems.title: Johnny shall have a new bonnet
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Johnny shall have a new bonnet,
  And Johnny shall go to the fair,
And Johnny shall have a blue ribbon
  To tie up his bonny brown hair.
And why may not I love Johnny?
  And why may not Johnny love me?
And why may not I love Johnny
  As well as another body?
And here's a leg for a stocking,
  And here is a leg for a shoe,
And he has a kiss for his daddy,
  And two for his mammy, I trow.
And why may not I love Johnny?
  And why may not Johnny love me?
And why may not I love Johnny,
  As well as another body?

poems.title: As I was walking o'er little Moorfields
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I was walking o'er little Moorfields,
I saw St. Paul's a running on wheels,
                With a fee, fo, fum.
Then for further frolics I'll go to France.
While Jack shall sing and his wife shall dance,
                With a fee, fo fum.

poems.title: The north wind doth blow
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
The north wind doth blow,
  And we shall have snow,
And what will poor Robin do then?
                    Poor thing!

  He'll sit in a barn,
  And to keep himself warm,
Will hide his head under his wing.
                    Poor thing!

poems.title: The white dove sat on the castle wall
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Songs. [From W. Wager's play, called 'The longer thou livest, the more foole thou art,' 4to, Lond.]

poems.title: Elsie Marley is grown so fine
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Elsie Marley is grown so fine,
She won't get up to serve the swine,
But lies in bed till eight or nine,
And surely she does take her time.

And do you ken Elsie Marley, honey?
The wife who sells the barley, honey;
She won't get up to serve her swine,
And do you ken Elsie Marley, honey?

poems.title: London bridge is broken down
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
London bridge is broken down,
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
London bridge is broken down,
  With a gay lady.

How shall we build it up again?
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
How shall we build it up again?
  With a gay lady.

Silver and gold will be stole away,
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
Silver and gold will be stole away,
  With a gay lady.

Build it up again with iron and steel,
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
Build it up with iron and steel,
  With a gay lady.

Iron and steel will bend and bow,
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
Iron and steel will bend and bow,
  With a gay lady.

Build it up with wood and clay,
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
Build it up with wood and clay,
  With a gay lady.

Wood and clay will wash away,
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
Wood and clay will wash away,
  With a gay lady.

Build it up with stone so strong,
  Dance o'er my lady lee;
Huzza! 'twill last for ages long,
  With a gay lady.

poems.title: Old Father of the Pye
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Old Father of the Pye,
I cannot sing, my lips are dry;
But when my lips are very well wet,
Then I can sing with the Heigh go Bet!

poems.title: Tom he was a piper's son
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Tom he was a piper's son,
He learn'd to play when he was young,
But all the tunes that he could play,
Was, "Over the hills and far away;"
Over the hills, and a great way off,
And the wind will blow my top-knot off.

Now Tom with his pipe made such a noise,
That he pleas'd both the girls and boys,
And they stopp'd to hear him play,
"Over the hills and far away."

Tom with his pipe did play with such skill,
That those who heard him could never keep still;
Whenever they heard they began for to dance,
Even pigs on their hind legs would after him prance.

As Dolly was milking her cow one day,
Tom took out his pipe and began for to play;
So Doll and the cow danced "the Cheshire round,"
Till the pail was broke, and the milk ran on the ground.

He met old dame Trot with a basket of eggs,
He used his pipe, and she used her legs;
She danced about till the eggs were all broke,
She began for to fret, but he laughed at the joke.

He saw a cross fellow was beating an ass,
Heavy laden with pots, pans, dishes, and glass;
He took out his pipe and played them a tune,
And the jackass's load was lightened full soon.

poems.title: Jacky, come give me thy fiddle
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Jacky, come give me thy fiddle,
  If ever thou mean to thrive:
Nay; I'll not give my fiddle
  To any man alive.

If I should give my fiddle,
  They'll think that I'm gone mad;
For many a joyful day
  My fiddle and I have had.

poems.title: Of all the gay birds that e'er I did see
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Of all the gay birds that e'er I did see,
The owl is the fairest by far to me;
For all the day long she sits on a tree,
And when the night comes away flies she.

poems.title: I love sixpence, pretty little sixpence
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
I love sixpence, pretty little sixpence,
  I love sixpence better than my life;
I spent a penny of it, I spent another,
  And took fourpence home to my wife.

Oh, my little fourpence, pretty little fourpence,
  I love fourpence better than my life;
I spent a penny of it, I spent another,
  And I took twopence home to my wife.

Oh, my little twopence, my pretty little twopence,
  I love twopence better than my life;
I spent a penny of it, I spent another,
  And I took nothing home to my wife.

Oh, my little nothing, my pretty little nothing,
  What will nothing buy for my wife?
I have nothing, I spend nothing,
  I love nothing better than my wife.

poems.title: Merry are the bells, and merry would they ring
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Merry are the bells, and merry would they ring,
Merry was myself, and merry could I sing;
With a merry ding-dong, happy, gay, and free,
And a merry sing-song, happy let us be!

Waddle goes your gait, and hollow are your hose,
Noddle goes your pate, and purple is your nose;
Merry is your sing-song, happy, gay, and free,
With a merry ding-dong, happy let us be!

Merry have we met, and merry have we been,
Merry let us part, and merry meet again;
With our merry sing-song, happy, gay, and free,
And a merry ding-dong, happy let us be!

poems.title: My maid Mary
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
My maid Mary
She minds her dairy,
    While I go a hoing and mowing each morn,
Merrily run the reel
And the little spinning wheel
    Whilst I am singing and mowing my corn.

poems.title: Hot-cross Buns!
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Hot-cross Buns!
    Hot-cross Buns!
One a penny, two a penny
    Hot-cross Buns!

    Hot-cross Buns!
    Hot-cross Buns!
If ye have no daughters,
    Give them to your sons.

poems.title: Wooley Foster has gone to sea
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Wooley Foster has gone to sea,
With silver buckles at his knee,
When he comes back he'll marry me,--
    Bonny Wooley Foster!

Wooley Foster has a cow,
Black and white about the mow,
Open the gates and let her through,
    Wooley Foster's ain cow!

Wooley Foster has a hen,
Cockle button, cockle ben,
She lay eggs for gentlemen,
    But none for Wooley Foster!

poems.title: Buz, quoth the blue fly
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Buz, quoth the blue fly,
  Hum, quoth the bee,
Buz and hum they cry,
  And so do we:
In his ear, in his nose,
  Thus, do you see?
He ate the dormouse,
  Else it was he.

poems.title: As I was going up the hill
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I was going up the hill,
  I met with Jack the piper,
And all the tunes that he could play
  Was "Tie up your petticoats tighter."

I tied them once, I tied them twice,
  I tied them three times over;
And all the songs that he could sing
  Was "Carry me safe to Dover."

poems.title: There were two birds sat on a stone
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: How does my lady's garden grow?
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
How does my lady's garden grow?
How does my lady's garden grow?
With cockle shells, and silver bells,
And pretty maids all of a row.

poems.title: There was a jolly miller (another version)
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was a jolly miller
  Lived on the river Dee:
He worked and sung from morn till night,
  No lark so blithe as he,
And this the burden of his song
  For ever used to be--
I jump mejerrime jee!
  I care for nobody--no! not I,
Since nobody cares for me.

poems.title: As I was going along, long, long
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I was going along, long, long,
A singing a comical song, song, song,
The lane that I went was so long, long, long,
And the song that I sung was as long, long, long,
And so I went singing along.

poems.title: Where are you going, my pretty maid?
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Where are you going, my pretty maid?
I'm going a-milking, sir, she said.
May I go with you, my pretty maid?
You're kindly welcome, sir, she said.
What is your father, my pretty maid?
My father's a farmer, sir, she said.

Say, will you marry me, my pretty maid?
Yes, if you please, kind sir, she said.
Will you be constant, my pretty maid?
That I can't promise you, sir, she said.
Then I won't marry you, my pretty maid!
Nobody asked you, sir! she said.

poems.title: Pancakes and fritters
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Songs. [Song on the bells of Derby on foot-ball morning, a custom now discontinued:]

poems.title: I have been to market, my lady, my lady
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: My father left me three acres of land
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
My father left me three acres of land,
  Sing ivy, sing ivy;
My father left me three acres of land,
  Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!

I ploughed it with a ram's horn,
  Sing ivy, sing ivy;
 And sowed it all over with one pepper corn,
  Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!

I harrowed it with a bramble bush,
  Sing ivy, sing ivy;
And reaped it with my little penknife,
  Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!

I got the mice to carry it to the barn,
  Sing ivy, &c.
And thrashed it with a goose's quill,
  Sing holly, &c.

I got the cat to carry it to the mill,
  Sing ivy, &c.
The miller he swore he would have her paw,
And the cat she swore she would scratch his face,
  Sing holly, go whistle and ivy!

poems.title: Three blind mice, see how they run!
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Three blind mice, see how they run!
They all ran after the farmer's wife,
Who cut off their tails with the carving-knife,
Did you ever see such fools in your life?
Three blind mice.

poems.title: There was a frog liv'd in a well
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was a frog liv'd in a well,
  Kitty alone, Kitty alone;
There was a frog liv'd in a well,
  Kitty alone, and I!

There was a frog liv'd in a well,
  And a farce mouse in a mill,
  Cock me cary, Kitty alone,
  Kitty alone, and I.

This frog he would a wooing ride,
  Kitty alone, &c.
This frog he would a wooing ride,
And on a snail he got astride,
  Cock me cary, &c.

He rode till he came to my Lady Mouse hall,
  Kitty alone, &c.
He rode till he came to my Lady Mouse hall,
And there he did both knock and call,
  Cock me cary, &c.

Quoth he, Miss Mouse, I'm come to thee,
  Kitty alone, &c.
Quoth he, Miss Mouse, I'm come to thee,
To see if thou canst fancy me,
  Cock me cary, &c.

Quoth she, answer I'll give you none,
  Kitty alone, &c.
Quoth she, answer I'll give you none,
Until my uncle Rat come home,
  Cock me cary, &c.

And when her uncle Rat came home,
  Kitty alone, &c.
And when her uncle Rat came home,
Who's been here since I've been gone?
  Cock me cary, &c.

Sir, there's been a worthy gentleman,
  Kitty alone, &c.
Sir, there's been a worthy gentleman,
That's been here since you've been gone,
  Cock me cary, &c.

The frog he came whistling through the brook,
  Kitty alone, &c.
The frog he came whistling through the brook,
And there he met with a dainty duck,
  Cock me cary, &c.

This duck she swallow'd him up with a pluck,
  Kitty alone, Kitty alone;
This duck she swallow'd him up with a pluck,
So there's an end of my history book.
  Cock me cary, Kitty alone,
  Kitty alone and I.

poems.title: There was a man in our toone, in our toone, in our toone
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was a man in our toone, in our toone, in our toone,
There was a man in our toone, and his name was Billy Pod;
And he played upon an old razor, an old razor, an old razor,
And he played upon an old razor, with my fiddle fiddle fe fum fo.

And his hat it was made of the good roast beef, the good roast beef,
        the good roast beef,
And his hat it was made of the good roast beef,
        and his name was Billy Pod;
And he played upon an old razor, &c.

And his coat it was made of the good fat tripe, the good fat tripe,
        the good fat tripe,
And his coat it was made of the good fat tripe,
        and his name was Billy Pod;
And he played upon an old razor, &c.

And his breeks were made of the bawbie baps, the bawbie baps,
    the bawbie baps,
And his breeks were made of the bawbie baps,
        and his name was Billy Pod;
And he played upon an old razor, &c.

And there was a man in tither toone, in tither toone, in tither
        toone,
And there was a man in tither toone, and his name was Edrin Drum;
And he played upon an old laadle, an old laadle, an old laadle,
And he played upon an old laadle, with my fiddle fiddle fe fum fo.

And he eat up all the good roast beef, the good roast beef, &c. &c.
And he eat up all the good fat tripe, the good fat tripe, &c. &c.
And he eat up all the bawbie baps, &c. and his name was Edrin Drum.

poems.title: John Cook had a little grey mare; he, haw, hum!
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
John Cook had a little grey mare; he, haw, hum!
Her back stood up, and her bones they were bare; he, haw, hum!

John Cook was riding up Shuter's bank; he, haw, hum!
And there his nag did kick and prank; he, haw, hum!

John Cook was riding up Shuter's hill; he, haw, hum!
His mare fell down, and she made her will; he, haw, hum!

The bridle and saddle were laid on the shelf; he, haw, hum!
If you want any more you may sing it yourself; he, haw, hum!

poems.title: A carrion crow sat on an oak
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
A carrion crow sat on an oak,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do,
Watching a tailor shape his cloak;
  Sing heigh ho, the carrion crow,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do.

Wife, bring me my old bent bow,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do,
That I may shoot yon carrion crow;
  Sing heigh ho, the carrion crow,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do.

The tailor he shot and missed his mark,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do,
And shot his own sow quite through the heart;
  Sing heigh ho, the carrion crow,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do.

Wife, bring brandy in a spoon,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do,
For our old sow is in a swoon;
  Sing heigh ho, the carrion crow,
  Fol de riddle, lol de riddle, hi ding do.

poems.title: Hic hoc, the carrion crow
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Songs. [Another version from MS. Sloane, 1489, fol. 17, written in the time of Charles I.]
poems.text:
Hic hoc, the carrion crow,
For I have shot something too low:
I have quite missed my mark,
And shot the poor sow to the heart;
Wife, bring treacle in a spoon,
Or else the poor sow's heart will down.

poems.title: Awa' birds, away!
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Songs. [Song of a little boy while passing his hour of solitude in a corn-field.]
poems.text:
Awa' birds, away!
Take a little, and leave a little,
And do not come again;
For if you do,
I will shoot you through,
And there is an end of you.

poems.title: If I'd as much money as I could spend
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: Whistle, daughter, whistle, whistle daughter dear
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: I'll sing you a song
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
I'll sing you a song,
Though not very long,
  Yet I think it as pretty as any,
Put your hand in your purse,
You'll never be worse,
  And give the poor singer a penny.

poems.title: Dame, get up and bake your pies
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Dame, get up and bake your pies,
Bake your pies, bake your pies;
Dame, get up and bake your pies,
On Christmas-day in the morning.

Dame, what makes your maidens lie,
Maidens lie, maidens lie;
Dame, what makes your maidens lie,
On Christmas-day in the morning?

Dame, what makes your ducks to die,
Ducks to die, ducks to die;
Dame, what makes your ducks to die,
On Christmas-day in the morning?

Their wings are cut and they cannot fly,
Cannot fly, cannot fly;
Their wings are cut and they cannot fly,
On Christmas-day in the morning.

poems.title: There was a girl in our towne
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was a girl in our towne,
Silk an' satin was her gowne,
Silk an' satin, gold an' velvet,
Guess her name, three times I've tell'd it.

poems.title: I went to the wood and got it
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
I went to the wood and got it,
I sat me down and looked at it;
The more I looked at it the less I liked it,
And I brought it home because I couldn't help it.

poems.title: Hick-a-more, Hack-a-more
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Hick-a-more, Hack-a-more,
On the king's kitchen-door;
All the king's horses,
And all the king's men,
Couldn't drive Hick-a-more, Hack-a-more,
Off the king's kitchen-door!

poems.title: When I was taken from the fair body
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
When I was taken from the fair body,
  They then cut off my head,
  And thus my shape was altered;
It's I that make peace between king and king,
  And many a true lover glad:
All this I do and ten times more,
  And more I could do still,
But nothing can I do,
  Without my guider's will.

poems.title: As I look'd out o' my chamber window
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I look'd out o' my chamber window
  I heard something fall;
I sent my maid to pick it up,
  But she couldn't pick it all.

poems.title: I went into my grandmother's garden
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
I went into my grandmother's garden,
And there I found a farthing.
I went into my next door neighbour's,
There I bought a pipkin and a popkin--
A slipkin and a slopkin,
A nailboard, a sailboard,
And all for a farthing.

poems.title: As I was going o'er London Bridge
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I was going o'er London Bridge,
I met a cart full of fingers and thumbs!

poems.title: Made in London
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Made in London,
Sold at York,
Stops a bottle
And is a cork.

poems.title: Ten and ten and twice eleven
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Ten and ten and twice eleven,
Take out six and put in seven;
Go to the green and fetch eighteen,
And drop one a coming.

poems.title: As soft as silk, as white as milk
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As soft as silk, as white as milk,
As bitter as gall, a thick wall,
And a green coat covers me all.

poems.title: As I was going o'er Tipple Tine
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Riddles. [A swarm of bees.]

poems.title: Humpty Dumpty lay in a beck
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Humpty Dumpty lay in a beck,
With all his sinews round his neck;
Forty doctors and forty wrights
Couldn't put Humpty Dumpty to rights!

poems.title: Arthur O'Bower has broken his band
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Riddles. [A storm of wind.]
poems.text:
Arthur O'Bower has broken his band,
He comes roaring up the land;--
The King of Scots, with all his power,
Cannot turn Arthur of the Bower!

poems.title: Make three-fourths of a cross
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: There was a king met a king
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was a king met a king
  In a narrow lane,
Says this king to that king,
  "Where have you been?"

"Oh! I've been a hunting
  With my dog and my doe."
"Pray lend him to me,
  That I may do so."

"There's the dog take the dog."
  "What's the dog's name?"
"I've told you already."
  "Pray tell me again."

poems.title: Flour of England, fruit of Spain
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Flour of England, fruit of Spain,
Met together in a shower of rain;
Put in a bag tied round with a string,
If you'll tell me this riddle, I'll give you a ring.

poems.title: Every lady in this land
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Every lady in this land
Has twenty nails upon each hand,
Five and twenty hands and feet,
All this is true without deceit.

poems.title: Twelve pears hanging high
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Twelve pears hanging high,
Twelve knights riding by;
Each knight took a pear,
And yet left eleven there!

poems.title: I have a little sister, they call her peep, peep
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: Old mother Twitchett had but one eye
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Riddles. [A needle and thread.]
poems.text:
Old mother Twitchett had but one eye,
And a long tail which she let fly;
And every time she went over a gap,
She left a bit of her tail in a trap.

poems.title: In marble walls as white as milk
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
In marble walls as white as milk,
Lined with a skin as soft as silk;
Within a fountain crystal clear,
A golden apple doth appear.
No doors there are to this strong-hold.
Yet things break in and steal the gold.

poems.title: What shoe-maker makes shoes without leather
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
What shoe-maker makes shoes without leather,
With all the four elements put together?
  Fire and water, earth and air;
  Ev'ry customer has two pair.

poems.title: Higgledy piggledy
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Higgledy piggledy
  Here we lie,
Pick'd and pluck'd,
  And put in a pie.
My first is snapping, snarling, growling,
My second's industrious, romping, and prowling.
Higgledy piggledy
  Here we lie,
Pick'd and pluck'd,
  And put in a pie.

poems.title: Thomas a Tattamus took two Ts
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Thomas a Tattamus took two Ts,
To tie two tups to two tall trees,
To frighten the terrible Thomas a Tattamus!
Tell me how many Ts there are in all THAT.

poems.title: There was a man who had no eyes
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Riddles. [The man had one eye, and the tree two apples upon it.]
poems.text:
There was a man who had no eyes,
He went abroad to view the skies;
He saw a tree with apples on it,
He took no apples off, yet left no apples on it.

poems.title: The moon nine days old
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
The moon nine days old,
The next sign to cancer;
Pat rat without a tail;--
And now, sir, for your answer,

poems.title: Little Nancy Etticoat
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Little Nancy Etticoat,
In a white petticoat,
And a red nose;
The longer she stands,
The shorter she grows.

poems.title: Long legs, crooked thighs
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Long legs, crooked thighs,
Little head and no eyes.

poems.title: There were three sisters in a hall
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Riddles. [From MS. Sloane, 1489, fol. 16, written in the time of Charles I.]
poems.text:
There were three sisters in a hall,
There came a knight amongst them all;
Good morrow, aunt, to the one,
Good morrow, aunt, to the other,
Good morrow, gentlewoman, to the third,
If you were my aunt,
  As the other two be,
I would say good morrow,
  Then, aunts, all three.

poems.title: Congeal'd water and Cain's brother
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Congeal'd water and Cain's brother,
That was my lover's name, and no other.

poems.title: Thirty white horses upon a red hill
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Thirty white horses upon a red hill,
Now they tramp, now they champ, now they stand still.

poems.title: Black we are, but much admired
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Black we are, but much admired;
Men seek for us till they are tired.
We tire the horse, but comfort man
Tell me this riddle if you can.

poems.title: Higher than a house, higher than a tree
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Higher than a house, higher than a tree;
Oh, whatever can that be?

poems.title: Humpty dumpty sate on a wall
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Humpty dumpty sate on a wall,
Humpty dumpty had a great fall;
Three score men and three score more
Cannot place Humpty Dumpty as he was before.

poems.title: Purple, yellow, red, and green
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Purple, yellow, red, and green,
The king cannot reach it nor the queen;
Nor can old Noll, whose power's so great:
Tell me this riddle while I count eight.

poems.title: Pease-porridge hot, pease-porridge cold
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Pease-porridge hot, pease-porridge cold,
Pease-porridge in the pot, nine days old.
Spell me that without a P,
And a clever scholar you will be.

poems.title: As I was going o'er Westminster bridge
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I was going o'er Westminster bridge,
  I met with a Westminster scholar;
He pulled off his cap an' drew off his glove,
  And wished me a very good morrow.
    What is his name?

poems.title: Black within, and red without
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Black within, and red without;
Four corners round about.

poems.title: There was a man rode through our town
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was a man rode through our town,
Gray Grizzle was his name;
His saddle-bow was gilt with gold,
Three times I've named his name.

poems.title: As I went over Lincoln bridge
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I went over Lincoln bridge
I met mister Rusticap;
Pins and needles on his back,
A going to Thorney fair.

poems.title: Two legs sat upon three legs
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Riddles. [One leg is a leg of mutton; two legs, a man; three legs, a stool; four legs, a dog.]
poems.text:
Two legs sat upon three legs,
With one leg in his lap;
In comes four legs,
And runs away with one leg.
Up jumps two legs,
Catches up three legs,
Throws it after four legs,
And makes him bring back one leg.

poems.title: Formed long ago, yet made to-day
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Formed long ago, yet made to-day,
  Employed while others sleep;
What few would like to give away,
  Nor any wish to keep.

poems.title: A riddle, a riddle, as I suppose
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
A riddle, a riddle, as I suppose,
A hundred eyes, and never a nose.

poems.title: As round as an apple, as deep as a cup
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As round as an apple, as deep as a cup,
And all the king's horses can't pull it up.

poems.title: As I went through the garden gap
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I went through the garden gap,
Who should I meet but Dick Red-cap!
A stick in his hand, a stone in his throat,
If you'll tell me this riddle, I'll give you a groat.

poems.title: Elizabeth, Elspeth, Betsy and Bess
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Elizabeth, Elspeth, Betsy and Bess,
They all went together to seek a bird's nest.
They found a bird's nest with five eggs in,
They all took one, and left four in.

poems.title: As I was going to St. Ives
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
As I was going to St. Ives,
I met a man with seven wives,
Every wife had seven sacks,
Every sack had seven cats,
Every cat had seven kits:
Kits, cats, sacks, and wives,
How many were there going to St. Ives?

poems.title: Highty, tighty, paradighty clothed in green
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Highty, tighty, paradighty clothed in green,
The king could not read it, no more could the queen;
They sent for a wise man out of the East,
Who said it had horns, but was not a beast!

poems.title: See, see! what shall I see?
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
See, see! what shall I see?
A horse's head where his tail should be.

poems.title: As I was going o'er London Bridge (another version)
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Riddles. [A fire-brand with sparks on it.]
poems.text:
As I was going o'er London Bridge,
  And peep'd through a nick,
I saw four and twenty ladies
  Riding on a stick!

poems.title: Lives in winter
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Lives in winter,
Dies in summer,
And grows with its root upwards!

poems.title: When I went up sandy hill
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
When I went up sandy hill,
I met a sandy boy;
I cut his throat, I sucked his blood,
And left his skin a hanging-o.

poems.title: I had a little castle upon the sea-side
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: Old father Graybeard
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Old father Graybeard,
  Without tooth or tongue;
If you'll give me your finger,
  I'll give you my thumb.

poems.title: Cushy cow bonny, let down thy milk
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Cushy cow bonny, let down thy milk,
And I will give thee a gown of silk;
A gown of silk and a silver tee,
If thou wilt let down thy milk to me.

poems.title: If you love me, pop and fly
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Charms. [Said to pips placed in the fire; a species of divination practised by children.]
poems.text:
If you love me, pop and fly;
If you hate me, lay and die.

poems.title: I went to the toad that lies under the wall
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
I went to the toad that lies under the wall,
I charmed him out, and he came at my call;
I scratch'd out the eyes of the owl before,
I tore the bat's wing, what would you have more.

poems.title: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John,
Guard the bed that I lay on!
  Four corners to my bed,
  Four angels round my head;
One to watch, one to pray,
And two to bear my soul away!

poems.title: Come, butter, come
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Come, butter, come,
Come, butter, come!
Peter stands at the gate,
Waiting for a butter'd cake;
Come, butter, come!

poems.title: When a Twister a twisting, will twist him a twist
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
When a Twister a twisting, will twist him a twist;
For the twisting of his twist, he three times doth intwist;
But if one of the twines of the twist do untwist,
The twine that untwisteth, untwisteth the twist.

Untwirling the twine that untwisteth between,
He twirls, with the twister, the two in a twine:
Then twice having twisted the twines of the twine
He twisteth the twine he had twined in twain.

The twain that, in twining, before in the twine,
As twines were intwisted; he now doth untwine:
'Twixt the twain inter-twisting a twine more between,
He, twirling his twister, makes a twist of the twine.

poems.title: A Thatcher of Thatchwood went to Thatchet a thatching
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
A Thatcher of Thatchwood went to Thatchet a thatching;
Did a thatcher of Thatchwood go to Thatchet a thatching?
If a thatcher of Thatchwood went to Thatchet a thatching,
Where's the thatching the thatcher of Thatchwood has thatch'd?

poems.title: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled pepper
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Charms. [Sometimes 'off a pewter plate' is added at the end of each line.]

poems.title: My father he left me, just as he was able
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
My father he left me, just as he was able,
One bowl, one bottle, one lable,
Two bowls, two bottles, two lables,
Three, &c.

poems.title: Robert Rowley rolled a round roll round
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: Three crooked cripples went through Cripplegate, and through
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Three crooked cripples went through Cripplegate, and through
Cripplegate went three crooked cripples.

poems.title: Swan swam over the sea
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Swan swam over the sea--
  Swim, swan, swim;
Swan swam back again,
  Well swam swan,

poems.title: Hickup, hickup, go away!
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Hickup, hickup, go away!
Come again another day;
Hickup, hickup, when I bake,
I'll give to you a butter-cake.

poems.title: Hickup, snicup
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Hickup, snicup,
Rise up, right up!
Three drops in the cup
Are good for the hiccup.

poems.title: There was an old woman, as I've heard tell
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman, as I've heard tell,
She went to market her eggs for to sell;
She went to market all on a market-day,
And she fell asleep on the king's highway.

There came by a pedlar whose name was Stout,
He cut her petticoats all round about;
He cut her petticoats up to the knees,
Which made the old woman to shiver and freeze.

When this little woman first did wake,
She began to shiver and she began to shake,
She began to wonder and she began to cry,
"Oh! deary, deary me, this is none of I!

"But if it be I, as I do hope it be,
I've a little dog at home, and he'll know me;
If it be I, he'll wag his little tail,
And if it be not I, he'll loudly bark and wail."

Home went the little woman all in the dark,
Up got the little dog, and he began to bark;
He began to bark, so she began to cry,
"Oh! deary, deary me, this is none of I!"

poems.title: There was an old woman who lived in a shoe
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman who lived in a shoe,
She had so many children she didn't know what to do;
She gave them some broth without any bread,
She whipped them all well and put them to bed.

poems.title: Old woman, old woman, shall we go a shearing?
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Old woman, old woman, shall we go a shearing?
Speak a little louder, sir, I am very thick of hearing.
Old woman, old woman, shall I love you dearly?
Thank you, kind sir, I hear you very clearly.

poems.title: There was an old woman sat spinning
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman sat spinning,
And that's the first beginning;
She had a calf,
And that's half;
She took it by the tail,
And threw it over the wall,
And that's all.

poems.title: There was an old woman, her name it was Peg
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman, her name it was Peg;
Her head was of wood, and she wore a cork-leg.
The neighbours all pitch'd her into the water,
Her leg was drown'd first, and her head follow'd a'ter.

poems.title: A little old man and I fell out
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
A little old man and I fell out;
How shall we bring this matter about?
Bring it about as well as you can,
Get you gone, you little old man!

poems.title: There was an old woman
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman,
  And she sold puddings and pies;
She went to the mill,
  And the dust flew in her eyes:
Hot pies and cold pies to sell!
  Wherever she goes,--
You may follow her by the smell.

poems.title: Old Mother Niddity Nod swore by the pudding-bag
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Old Mother Niddity Nod swore by the pudding-bag,
  She would go to Stoken Church fair;
And then old Father Peter said he would meet her
  Before she got half-way there.

poems.title: There was an old woman (another version)
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman
  Lived under a hill;
And if she's not gone,
  She lives there still.

poems.title: There was an old woman toss'd up in a basket
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman toss'd up in a basket
  Nineteen times as high as the moon;
Where she was going I couldn't but ask it,
  For in her hand she carried a broom.

Old woman, old woman, old woman, quoth I,
  O whither, O whither, O whither, so high?
To brush the cobwebs off the sky!
  Shall I go with thee? Aye, by and by.

poems.title: There was an old man who liv'd in Middle Row
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old man who liv'd in Middle Row,
He had five hens and a name for them, oh!
Bill and Ned and Battock,
Cut-her-foot and Pattock,
Chuck, my lady Prattock,
Go to thy nest and lay.

poems.title: There was an old woman of Leeds
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman of Leeds
Who spent all her time in good deeds;
  She worked for the poor
  Till her fingers were sore,
This pious old woman of Leeds!

poems.title: Old Betty Blue
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Old Betty Blue
    Lost a holiday shoe,
What can old Betty do?
    Give her another
    To match the other,
And then she may swagger in two.

poems.title: Old mother Hubbard
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Old mother Hubbard
Went to the cupboard,
  To get her poor dog a bone;
But when she came there
  The cupboard was bare,
And so the poor dog had none.

She went to the baker's
  To buy him some bread,
But when she came back
  The poor dog was dead.

She went to the joiner's
  To buy him a coffin,
But when she came back
  The poor dog was laughing.

She took a clean dish
  To get him some tripe,
But when she came back
  He was smoking his pipe.

She went to the fishmonger's
  To buy him some fish,
And when she came back
  He was licking the dish.

She went to the ale-house
  To get him some beer,
But when she came back
  The dog sat in a chair.

She went to the tavern
  For white wine and red,
But when she came back
  The dog stood on his head.

She went to the hatter's
  To buy him a hat,
But when she came back
  He was feeding the cat.

She went to the barber's
  To buy him a wig,
But when she came back
  He was dancing a jig.

She went to the fruiterer's
  To buy him some fruit,
But when she came back
  He was playing the flute.

She went to the tailor's
  To buy him a coat,
But when she came back
  He was riding a goat.

She went to the cobbler's
  To buy him some shoes,
But when she came back
  He was reading the news.

She went to the sempstress
  To buy him some linen,
But when she came back
  The dog was spinning.

She went to the hosier's
  To buy him some hose,
But when she came back
  He was dress'd in his clothes.

The dame made a curtsey,
  The dog made a bow;
The dame said, your servant,
  The dog said, bow, wow.

poems.title: There was an old woman (another version, 3)
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman
  Lived under a hill,
She put a mouse in a bag,
  And sent it to mill;

The miller declar'd
  By the point of his knife,
He never took toll
  Of a mouse in his life.

poems.title: There was an old woman had three sons
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman had three sons,
Jerry, and James, and John:
Jerry was hung, James was drowned,
John was lost and never was found,
And there was an end of the three sons,
Jerry, and James, and John!

poems.title: There was an old man, who lived in a wood
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old man, who lived in a wood,
  As you may plainly see;
He said he could do as much work in a day,
  As his wife could do in three.
With all my heart, the old woman said,
  If that you will allow,
To-morrow you'll stay at home in my stead,
  And I'll go drive the plough:

But you must milk the Tidy cow,
  For fear that she go dry;
And you must feed the little pigs
  That are within the sty;
And you must mind the speckled hen,
  For fear she lay away;
And you must reel the spool of yarn
  That I spun yesterday.

The old woman took a staff in her hand,
  And went to drive the plough:
The old man took a pail in his hand,
  And went to milk the cow;
But Tidy hinched, and Tidy flinched,
  And Tidy broke his nose,
And Tidy gave him such a blow,
  That the blood ran down to his toes.

High! Tidy! ho! Tidy! high!
  Tidy! do stand still;
If ever I milk you, Tidy, again,
  'Twill be sore against my will!
He went to feed the little pigs,
  That were within the sty;
He hit his head against the beam,
  And he made the blood to fly.

He went to mind the speckled hen,
  For fear she'd lay astray,
And he forgot the spool of yarn
  His wife spun yesterday.

So he swore by the sun, the moon, and the stars,
  And the green leaves on the tree,
If his wife didn't do a day's work in her life,
  She should ne'er be ruled by he.

poems.title: There was an old man of Tobago
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old man of Tobago,
Who lived on rice, gruel, and sago;
  Till, much to his bliss,
  His physician said this--
"To a leg, sir, of mutton you may go."

poems.title: Oh, dear, what can the matter be?
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Oh, dear, what can the matter be?
Two old women got up in an apple tree;
One came down,
And the other staid till Saturday.

poems.title: There was an old man
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: Father Short came down the lane
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Father Short came down the lane,
  Oh! I'm obliged to hammer and smite
  From four in the morning till eight at night,
For a bad master, and a worse dame.

poems.title: There was an old woman called Nothing-at-all
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman called Nothing-at-all,
Who rejoiced in a dwelling exceedingly small:
A man stretched his mouth to its utmost extent,
And down at one gulp house and old woman went.

poems.title: There was an old woman of Norwich
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman of Norwich,
Who lived upon nothing but porridge;
  Parading the town,
  She turned cloak into gown,
This thrifty old woman of Norwich.

poems.title: A little old man of Derby
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
A little old man of Derby,
How do you think he served me?
He took away my bread and cheese,
And that is how he served me.

poems.title: There was an old woman in Surrey
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There was an old woman in Surrey,
Who, was morn, noon, and night in a hurry;
    Call'd her husband a fool,
    Drove the children to school,
The worrying old woman of Surrey.

poems.title: One-ery, two-ery
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Games. [Rhymes used by children to decide who is to begin a game.]
poems.text:
One-ery, two-ery,
  Ziccary zan;
Hollow bone, crack a bone,
  Ninery, ten:
Spittery spot,
  It must be done;
Twiddleum twaddleum,
  Twenty-one.

Hink spink, the puddings stink,
  The fat begins to fry,
Nobody at home, but jumping Joan,
  Father, mother, and I.
Stick, stock, stone dead,
  Blind man can't see,
Every knave will have a slave,
  You or I must be he.

poems.title: Who goes round my house this night?
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Who goes round my house this night?
  None but cruel Tom!
Who steals all the sheep at night?
  None but this poor one.

poems.title: Dance, Thumbkin, dance
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text: Dance, Thumbkin, dance,

poems.title: One to make ready
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Games. [The following is used by schoolboys, when two are starting to run a race.]
poems.text:
One to make ready,
  And two to prepare;
Good luck to the rider,
  And away goes the mare.

poems.title: Gay go up and gay go down
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Gay go up and gay go down,
To ring the bells of London town.

Bull's eyes and targets,
Say the bells of St. Marg'ret's.

Brickbats and tiles,
Say the bells of St. Giles'.

Halfpence and farthings,
Say the bells of St. Martin's.

Oranges and lemons,
Say the bells of St. Clement's.

Pancakes and fritters,
Say the bells of St. Peter's.

Two sticks and an apple,
Say the bells at Whitechapel.

Old Father Baldpate,
Say the slow bells at Aldgate.

You owe me ten shillings,
Say the bells at St. Helen's.

Pokers and tongs,
Say the bells at St. John's.

Kettles and pans,
Say the bells at St. Ann's.

When will you pay me?
Say the bells at Old Bailey.

When I grow rich,
Say the bells at Shoreditch.

Pray when will that be?
Say the bells of Stepney.

I am sure I don't know,
Says the great bell at Bow.

Here comes a candle to light you to bed,
And here comes a chopper to chop off your head.

poems.title: Buff says Buff to all his men
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Buff says Buff to all his men,
And I say Buff to you again;
Buff neither laughs nor smiles,
But carries his face
With a very good grace,
And passes the stick to the very next place!

poems.title: Pease-pudding hot
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Games. [Game with the hands.]
poems.text:
Pease-pudding hot,
  Pease-pudding cold,
Pease-pudding in the pot,
  Nine days old.
Some like it hot,
  Some like it cold,
Some like it in the pot,
  Nine days old.

poems.title: Awake, arise, pull out your eyes
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Awake, arise, pull out your eyes,
  And hear what time of day;
And when you have done, pull out your tongue,
  And see what you can say.

poems.title: Twelve huntsmen with horns and hounds
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Games. [This game begins thus: Take this--What's this?--A gaping, wide-mouthed, waddling frog, &c.]

poems.title: A.  Draw a pail of water
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
A.  Draw a pail of water,
    For my lady's daughter;
    My father's a king, and my mother's a queen,
    My two little sisters are dress'd in green,
    Stamping grass and parsley,
    Marigold leaves and daisies.
B.  One rush, two rush,
    Pray thee, fine lady, come under my bush.

poems.title: Sieve my lady's oatmeal
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Sieve my lady's oatmeal,
  Grind my lady's flour,
Put it in a chesnut,
  Let it stand an hour;
One may rush, two may rush,
Come, my girls, walk under the bush.

poems.title: Queen Anne, queen Anne, you sit in the sun
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Queen Anne, queen Anne, you sit in the sun,
As fair as a lily, as white as a wand.
I send you three letters, and pray read one,
You must read one, if you can't read all,
So pray, Miss or Master, throw up the ball.

poems.title: There were three jovial Welshmen
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There were three jovial Welshmen,
  As I have heard them say,
And they would go a-hunting
  Upon St. David's day.

All the day they hunted,
  And nothing could they find
But a ship a-sailing,
  A-sailing with the wind.

One said it was a ship,
  The other he said, nay;
The third said it was a house,
  With the chimney blown away.

And all the night they hunted,
  And nothing could they find
But the moon a-gliding,
  A-gliding with the wind.

One said it was the moon,
  The other he said, nay;
The third said it was a cheese,
  And half o't cut away.

And all the day they hunted,
  And nothing could they find
But a hedgehog in a bramble bush,
  And that they left behind.

The first said it was a hedgehog,
  The second he said, nay;
The third it was a pincushion,
  And the pins stuck in wrong way.

And all the night they hunted,
  And nothing could they find
But a hare in a turnip field,
  And that they left behind.

The first said it was a hare,
  The second he said, nay;
The third said it was a calf,
  And the cow had run away.

And all the day they hunted,
  And nothing could they find
But an owl in a holly tree,
  And that they left behind.

One said it was an owl,
  The other he said, nay;
The third said 'twas an old man,
  And his beard growing grey.

poems.title: Is John Smith within?
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Is John Smith within?--
Yes, that he is.
Can he set a shoe?--
Ay, marry, two,
Here a nail, there a nail,
Tick, tack, too.

poems.title: Margery Mutton-pie, and Johnny Bopeep
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Margery Mutton-pie, and Johnny Bopeep,
They met together in Grace-church Street;
In and out, in and out, over the way,
Oh! says Johnny, 'tis chop-nose day.

poems.title: Intery, mintery, cutery-corn
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Intery, mintery, cutery-corn,
Apple seed and apple thorn;
Wine, brier, limber-lock,
Five geese in a flock,
Sit and sing by a spring,
O-U-T, and in again.

poems.title: A duck and a drake
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
A duck and a drake,
    A nice barley-cake,
With a penny to pay the old baker;
    A hop and a scotch,
    Is another notch,
Slitherum, slatherum, take her.

poems.title: See, Saw, Margery Daw
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
See, Saw, Margery Daw,
Sold her bed and lay upon straw;
Was not she a dirty slut,
To sell her bed and lie in the dirt!

poems.title: See, saw, Margery Daw
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
See, saw, Margery Daw,
  Little Jackey shall have a new master;
Little Jackey shall have but a penny a day,
  Because he can't work any faster.

poems.title: I am a gold lock.
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
I am a gold lock.
I am a gold key.
I am a silver lock.
I am a silver key.
I am a brass lock.
I am a brass key.
I am a lead lock.
I am a lead key.
I am a monk lock.
I am a monk key!

poems.title: Ride a cock-horse to Banbury-cross
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Ride a cock-horse to Banbury-cross,
To buy little Johnny a galloping-horse;
It trots behind, and it ambles before,
And Johnny shall ride till he can ride no more.

poems.title: Ride a cock-horse to Banbury-cross (another version)
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Ride a cock-horse to Banbury-cross,
  To see what Tommy can buy;
A penny white loaf, a penny white cake,
  And a twopenny apple-pie.

poems.title: Jack be nimble
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Jack be nimble,
  And Jack be quick:
And Jack jump over
  The candle-stick.

poems.title: Weave the diaper tick-a-tick tick
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Weave the diaper tick-a-tick tick,
Weave the diaper tick--
Come this way, come that
As close as a mat,
Athwart and across, up and down, round about,
And forwards, and backwards, and inside, and out;
Weave the diaper thick-a-thick thick,
Weave the diaper thick!

poems.title: One-ery, two-ery, hickary, hum
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Games. [Used in Somersetshire in counting out the game of pee-wip or pee wit.]
poems.text:
One-ery, two-ery, hickary, hum,
Fillison, follison, Nicholson, John,
Quever, quauver, Irish Mary,
Stenkarum, stankarum, buck!

poems.title: Whoop, whoop, and hollow
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Whoop, whoop, and hollow,
Good dogs won't follow,
Without the hare cries "pee wit."

poems.title: Tom Brown's two little Indian boys
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Tom Brown's two little Indian boys,
  One ran away,
  The other wouldn't stay,--
Tom Brown's two little Indian boys.

poems.title: There were two blackbirds
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
There were two blackbirds,
    Sitting on a hill,
The one nam'd Jack,
    The other nam'd Jill;
  Fly away Jack!
  Fly away Jill!
  Come again Jack!
  Come again Jill!

poems.title: Tip, top, tower
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Tip, top, tower,
Tumble down in an hour.

poems.title: I went up one pair of stairs.
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
I went up one pair of stairs.
Just like me.
I went up two pair of stairs.
Just like me.
I went into a room.
Just like me.
I looked out of a window.
Just like me.
And there I saw a monkey.
Just like me.

poems.title: Number number nine, this hoop's mine
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Number number nine, this hoop's mine;
Number number ten, take it back again.

poems.title: Here goes my lord
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Here goes my lord
A trot, a trot, a trot, a trot,
  Here goes my lady
A canter, a canter, a canter, a canter!
    Here goes my young master
  Jockey-hitch, Jockey-hitch, Jockey-hitch, Jockey-hitch:
    Here goes my young miss,
  An amble, an amble, an amble, an amble!
The footman lays behind to tipple ale and wine,
And goes gallop, a gallop, a gallop, to make up his time.

poems.title: Green cheese, yellow laces
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Green cheese, yellow laces,
Up and down the market-places,
  Turn, cheeses, turn!

poems.title: To market ride the gentlemen
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: Ride a cock-horse to Coventry-cross
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)

poems.title: Ride a cock-horse to Banbury-cross (another version, 3)
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Ride a cock-horse to Banbury-cross,
To see an old lady upon a white horse,
Rings on her fingers, and bells on her toes,
And so she makes music wherever she goes.

poems.title: Let us go to the wood, says this pig
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.note: Halliwell's class: Games. [Song set to five toes.]

poems.title: Ring me (1), ring me (2), ring me rary (3)
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
Ring me (1), ring me (2), ring me rary (3),
As I go round (4), ring by ring (5),
A virgin (6) goes a maying (7),
Here's a flower (8), and there's a flower (9),
Growing in my lady's garden (10),
If you set your foot awry (11),
Gentle John will make you cry (12),
If you set your foot amiss (13),
Gentle John (14) will give you a kiss.

This [lady or gentleman] is none of ours,
Has put [him or her] self in [the selected child's] power,
So clap all hands, and ring all bells, and make the wedding o'er.

poems.title: Two broken tradesmen
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poems.collection: The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by J. O. Halliwell (London: Warne; first ed. 1842; this printing 1886)
poems.text:
"Two broken tradesmen,
  Newly come over,
The one from France and Scotland,
  The other from Dover."
"What's your trade?"

poems.title: Clap hands, clap hands
poems.author: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
